author: show-me state times
title: Dustin May nearly throws no-hitter in Cardinals' loss to Brewers in Milwaukee
text:
Dustin May returned to American Family Field in Milwaukee on May 27, pitching for the St. Louis Cardinals for the first time at the stadium since suffering a significant elbow injury there in 2021. In his previous appearance at this venue, May exited after one pitch due to pain and later underwent Tommy John surgery, which limited him to just 78 innings over three years before he resumed full-time play in 2025.
In Wednesday’s game, May came close to making history by taking a no-hitter into the eighth inning during a 2-1 loss against the Brewers. It was his most dominant start as a professional, becoming only the second Cardinals starter this season to complete seven innings. “That was definitely on my mind as I was warming up,” Dustin May said about returning from injury. “Funny as it is, I was praying like, ‘Let’s please not have this happen again.’ Because it had been so long since I have been here, but yeah, it was good to go out and get a good one.”
May retired 15 straight batters after catcher’s interference allowed Sal Frelick on base in the third inning. The only other Brewer who reached base before the eighth did so when Jake Bauers was hit by a pitch in the second inning. Garrett Mitchell broke up the no-hit bid with a leadoff double in the eighth; Luis Rengifo then bunted for an infield single that put runners at first and third with none out and ended May’s outing.
“It’s hard to not at least be a thought, but you try and push it out as much as possible,” May said of thinking about throwing a no-hitter. “At that point, you’re just trying to win a ballgame. It’s a 1-0 game, trying to go out and execute pitches outside of that.” JoJo Romero relieved him but could not preserve either lead or shutout; Christian Yelich tied it with an RBI single before Masyn Winn mishandled Jackson Chourio’s grounder, allowing another run.
The Cardinals’ last no-hitter remains Bud Smith’s performance on September 3, 2001 against the San Diego Padres—the only complete game of Smith’s career. Winn praised his teammate: “[May] was electric. Gave us the best chance he could to win,” Winn said. “That was definitely fun to watch. That’s the best I’ve seen him throw.”
Despite multiple surgeries—including Tommy John surgery followed by flexor tendon repair and an emergency esophagus procedure—May has recently shown improved form with increased velocity late into games and has gone six or more innings while allowing three or fewer runs in seven of his past nine starts.
Reflecting on his progress since returning from injuries that delayed his career trajectory, “I would like to say that I’m relatively close to the same pitcher I was, but I’m not. My stuff was better then,” May said. “It’s kind of how it was, but I feel good to be where I’m at and lucky to be here.”
